text: Chapter 3 teaches harmonic minor as an active, cadential scale used to build single-line melodies over tension-and-resolution chord progressions, particularly V7–I cadences ending on minor or major chords. The core techniques include: understanding the harmonic minor scale's built-in dominant function; adding the minor 7th as a non-scale color tone (inherited from aeolian); deriving scale arpeggios by replacing the perfect 5th with #5 (in major arpeggios) and the minor 7th with major 7th (in minor arpeggios); and embedding chromatic approach notes ascending between these arpeggios to create a 'chromatic illusion' of multiple scales. Two symmetric harmonic structures — the diminished chord (as rootless V7(b9)) and the augmented chord — each provide four enharmonic spellings that function transparently within the dominant chord, and both are used as melodic cells rather than consecutive harmonic material. The method establishes five vertical fretboard zones anchored to guide chords (Cm(maj7) and Eb+(maj7)), introduces the concept of 'active' vs 'static' scales distinguished by the 6th degree, and enforces strict rules: the resolution note must match the destination chord; the natural 6 is forbidden over V7–Im cadences; descending augmented arpeggios require horizontal alternate picking (the George Benson technique); and chord-family superimposition over the dominant avoids landing on the tonic root. Load-bearing terminology includes harmonic minor, Ionian (#5), chromatic illusion, fake diminished chords, augmented chords, and degree substitution, all governed by the foundational principle that melodic decisions must respect both scale function and harmonic context.
